claim: Parent and offspring are in conflict over how much parents should invest in their young where offspring typically demand more than is optimal for the parent.
source: However, parent and offspring are in conflict over how much parents should invest in their young where offspring typically demand more than is optimal for the parent (Trivers, 1974; Godfray, 1995), and the existence of this genetic conflict has been demonstrated in empirical research (Kölliker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Trivers (1974), Godfray (1995), and Kölliker et al. (2015)

claim: The existence of genetic conflict between parent and offspring has been demonstrated in empirical research.
source: However, parent and offspring are in conflict over how much parents should invest in their young where offspring typically demand more than is optimal for the parent (Trivers, 1974; Godfray, 1995), and the existence of this genetic conflict has been demonstrated in empirical research (Kölliker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kölliker et al. (2015)

claim: Selection pressures are predicted to lead to the evolution of traits in offspring that influence parental behaviour.
source: The resulting selection pressures are predicted to lead to the evolution of traits in offspring that influence parental behaviour (and thus investment).
evidence: Based on theoretical predictions from parent-offspring conflict theory

claim: Parental traits should be selected for their effects on offspring traits that influence parental behaviour indirectly.
source: Conversely, parental traits should be selected for their effects on offspring traits that influence parental behaviour indirectly (Kilner and Hinde, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kilner and Hinde (2012)

claim: Specific combinations of demand and provisioning are selectively favoured according to coadaptation models.
source: The correlation between parental and offspring traits has been the focus of coadaptation models where specific combinations of demand and provisioning are selectively favoured (Wolf and Brodie III, 1998; Kölliker et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wolf and Brodie III (1998) and Kölliker et al. (2005)

claim: Genetic variation in offspring exists for traits that indirectly influence maternal investment.
source: The fundamental assumption underlying predictions about the evolution of traits involved in parent-offspring interactions is that genetic variation in offspring exists for traits that indirectly influence maternal investment and vice versa.
evidence: Stated as a fundamental assumption of theoretical models

claim: It remains to be shown whether specific genetic variants in offspring indirectly influence maternal behaviour.
source: However, it remains to be shown whether specific genetic variants in offspring indirectly influence maternal behaviour.
evidence: Statement about gap in knowledge prior to this study

claim: Genes expressed in offspring modify the quality of maternal behaviour and thus affect, indirectly, offspring fitness.
source: In an experimental mouse population, we demonstrate that genes expressed in offspring modify the quality of maternal behaviour and thus affect, indirectly, offspring fitness.
evidence: Primary finding of the study based on experimental data

claim: A cross-fostering experiment was conducted between genetically variable and genetically uniform mice using the BXD mouse population.
source: To investigate the genetics of parent-offspring interactions we conducted a cross-fostering experiment between genetically variable and genetically uniform mice, using the largest genetic reference panel in mammals, the BXD mouse population.
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: The BXD mouse population is the largest genetic reference panel in mammals.
source: To investigate the genetics of parent-offspring interactions we conducted a cross-fostering experiment between genetically variable and genetically uniform mice, using the largest genetic reference panel in mammals, the BXD mouse population.
evidence: Statement about the BXD population

claim: Families of genetically variable mothers and genetically uniform offspring were generated by cross-fostering C57BL/6J (B6) litters to mothers of a given BXD strain.
source: We generated families of genetically variable mothers and genetically uniform offspring by cross-fostering C57BL/6J (B6) litters, in which no genetic variation occurs between animals of this strain, to mothers of a given BXD strain.
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: No genetic variation occurs between animals of the C57BL/6J strain.
source: We generated families of genetically variable mothers and genetically uniform offspring by cross-fostering C57BL/6J (B6) litters, in which no genetic variation occurs between animals of this strain, to mothers of a given BXD strain.
evidence: Statement about inbred strain characteristics

claim: BXD female litters were cross-fostered to B6 mothers.
source: Conversely, a BXD female's litter was cross-fostered to B6 mothers (Figure 1).
evidence: Description of experimental design with reference to Figure 1

claim: The cross-fostering design allows analysis of the effects of genetic variation in mothers or offspring while controlling for genetic variation in the other.
source: Thus, we can analyse the effects of genetic variation in mothers or offspring while controlling for genetic variation in the other.
evidence: Explanation of experimental design logic

claim: Cross-fostering design breaks the correlation between maternal and offspring traits.
source: This cross-fostering design has been successfully utilized in previous studies on family interactions because it breaks the correlation between maternal and offspring traits.
evidence: Explanation of cross-fostering methodology

claim: Different families or naturally occurring variation of maternal and offspring trait combinations across different broods are assumed to represent distinct evolved strategies.
source: Here, different families, or naturally occurring variation of maternal and offspring trait combinations across different broods, are assumed to represent distinct evolved strategies (Agrawal et al., 2001; Hager and Johnstone, 2003; Meunier and Kölliker, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Agrawal et al. (2001), Hager and Johnstone (2003), and Meunier and Kölliker (2012)

claim: Offspring and maternal body weights and behaviour were recorded from birth until weaning at 3 weeks of age.
source: From birth until weaning at 3 weeks of age we recorded offspring and maternal body weights and behaviour, following Hager and Johnstone (2003).
evidence: Description of data collection methods

claim: A total of 42 BXD lines with three within-line repeats plus the corresponding B6 families were set up for the experiment.
source: A total of 42 BXD lines with three within-line repeats plus the corresponding B6 families were set up for the experiment.
evidence: Description of experimental design shown in Figure 1 caption

claim: Variation in offspring genotype affects maternal behaviour.
source: We found that variation in offspring genotype affects maternal behaviour, which in turn influences offspring development and fitness.
evidence: Primary finding from genetic mapping analysis

claim: Maternal behaviour influences offspring development and fitness.
source: We found that variation in offspring genotype affects maternal behaviour, which in turn influences offspring development and fitness.
evidence: Finding from the study based on data analysis

claim: A locus on offspring chromosome 7 (OspIge7.1) modifies maternal nestbuilding on day 6.
source: During the first postnatal week we mapped a locus on offspring chromosome 7, OspIge7.1, modifying maternal nestbuidling on day 6 (Figure 2).
evidence: Genetic mapping result shown in Figure 2

claim: At the OspIge7.1 locus, the D2 allele increases maternal nestbuilding such that B6 mothers showed more nestbuilding activity when fostering BXD pups carrying the D2 allele.
source: At this locus, the D2 allele increases the trait value such that B6 mothers showed more nestbuilding activity when fostering BXD pups carrying the D2 allele at the locus.
evidence: Genetic mapping result describing allelic effects

claim: Nestbuilding is particularly important for offspring fitness as thermoregulation is underdeveloped and hypothermia is the primary cause of early death, even if milk is supplied.
source: Nestbuilding is particularly important for offspring fitness as thermoregulation is underdeveloped and hypothermia is the primary cause of early death, even if milk is supplied (Lynch and Possidente, 1978).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lynch and Possidente (1978)

claim: A locus on offspring distal chromosome 5 (OspIge5.1) affects maternal behaviour on day 14.
source: We detected a further locus on offspring distal chromosome 5 (OspIge5.1) that affects maternal behaviour on day 14, around the time we expect the weaning conflict to be highest (Figure 3).
evidence: Genetic mapping result shown in Figure 3

claim: Day 14 is around the time when weaning conflict is expected to be highest.
source: We detected a further locus on offspring distal chromosome 5 (OspIge5.1) that affects maternal behaviour on day 14, around the time we expect the weaning conflict to be highest (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on knowledge of mouse development and weaning conflict theory

claim: At the OspIge5.1 locus, mothers showed increased levels of maternal behaviour when fostering BXD offspring carrying the D2 allele.
source: Here, mothers showed increased levels of maternal behaviour when fostering BXD offspring carrying the D2 allele.
evidence: Genetic mapping result describing allelic effects

claim: Offspring growth during the second week is affected by a locus on maternal chromosome 17 (MatIge17.1).
source: Here, we found that offspring growth during the second week is affected by a locus on maternal chromosome 17, MatIge17.1, where the B6 allele increases the trait value (Figure 4).
evidence: Genetic mapping result shown in Figure 4

claim: At the MatIge17.1 locus, the B6 allele increases offspring growth during the second week.
source: Here, we found that offspring growth during the second week is affected by a locus on maternal chromosome 17, MatIge17.1, where the B6 allele increases the trait value (Figure 4).
evidence: Genetic mapping result describing allelic effects shown in Figure 4

claim: A direct genetic effect locus for maternal behaviour was found on proximal chromosome 10 (MatDge10.1).
source: In mothers we found a direct genetic effect locus for maternal behaviour on proximal chromosome 10, and for nestbuilding behaviour on chromosome 1 (MatDge10.1 and MatDge1.1, respectively), where the B6 allele increases the trait value in both cases.
evidence: Genetic mapping result

claim: A direct genetic effect locus for nestbuilding behaviour was found on chromosome 1 (MatDge1.1).
source: In mothers we found a direct genetic effect locus for maternal behaviour on proximal chromosome 10, and for nestbuilding behaviour on chromosome 1 (MatDge10.1 and MatDge1.1, respectively), where the B6 allele increases the trait value in both cases.
evidence: Genetic mapping result

claim: At the MatDge10.1 and MatDge1.1 loci, the B6 allele increases the trait value in both cases.
source: In mothers we found a direct genetic effect locus for maternal behaviour on proximal chromosome 10, and for nestbuilding behaviour on chromosome 1 (MatDge10.1 and MatDge1.1, respectively), where the B6 allele increases the trait value in both cases.
evidence: Genetic mapping result describing allelic effects

claim: A locus for offspring solicitation behaviour was detected on chromosome 5 (OspDge5.1) with the D2 allele increasing the level of solicitation shown.
source: We also detected a locus for offspring solicitation behaviour on chromosome 5 (OspDge5.1) with the D2 allele increasing the level of solicitation shown.
evidence: Genetic mapping result

claim: The OspDge5.1 locus is located at the opposite end of chromosome 5 from where OspIge5.1 is located.
source: Its location is at the opposite end on chromosome 5 from where OspIge5.1 is located.
evidence: Comparison of genetic mapping results

claim: Indirect genetic effects (IGEs) and direct genetic effects (DGEs) can be linked to specific loci that affect parent-offspring interaction.
source: Overall, our results show that IGEs, as well as DGEs, can be linked to specific loci that affect parent-offspring interaction, and it is thus possible that selection may occur on genes with indirect and direct effects on parental behaviour.
evidence: Summary of genetic mapping results

claim: Selection may occur on genes with indirect and direct effects on parental behaviour.
source: Overall, our results show that IGEs, as well as DGEs, can be linked to specific loci that affect parent-offspring interaction, and it is thus possible that selection may occur on genes with indirect and direct effects on parental behaviour.
evidence: Inference from genetic mapping results

claim: Variation in maternal behaviour is affected by genes expressed in offspring at the phenotypic level.
source: Importantly, our result that variation in maternal behaviour is affected by genes expressed in offspring is also clearly borne out at the phenotypic level: offspring solicitation behaviour in genetically variable BXD pups is positively correlated with the level of maternal behaviour in their genetically uniform B6 adoptive mothers on all three days we measured behaviour with significant effects of maternal behaviour and day on offspring solicitation (GLM, F1,103 = 17.62, P < 0.001 and F2,103 = 14.22, P < 0.001, respectively; day 6: Pearsons'r = 0.56, P = 0.003; day 10: r = 0.63, P = 0.001, and day 14: r = 0.55, P = 0.008; Supplementary file 2, a).
evidence: Statistical analysis of phenotypic correlations

claim: Offspring solicitation behaviour in genetically variable BXD pups is positively correlated with the level of maternal behaviour in their genetically uniform B6 adoptive mothers on all three days measured.
source: Importantly, our result that variation in maternal behaviour is affected by genes expressed in offspring is also clearly borne out at the phenotypic level: offspring solicitation behaviour in genetically variable BXD pups is positively correlated with the level of maternal behaviour in their genetically uniform B6 adoptive mothers on all three days we measured behaviour with significant effects of maternal behaviour and day on offspring solicitation (GLM, F1,103 = 17.62, P < 0.001 and F2,103 = 14.22, P < 0.001, respectively; day 6: Pearsons'r = 0.56, P = 0.003; day 10: r = 0.63, P = 0.001, and day 14: r = 0.55, P = 0.008; Supplementary file 2, a).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant correlations on days 6, 10, and 14

claim: Maternal behaviour and day have significant effects on offspring solicitation behaviour (GLM, F1,103 = 17.62, P < 0.001 and F2,103 = 14.22, P < 0.001).
source: offspring solicitation behaviour in genetically variable BXD pups is positively correlated with the level of maternal behaviour in their genetically uniform B6 adoptive mothers on all three days we measured behaviour with significant effects of maternal behaviour and day on offspring solicitation (GLM, F1,103 = 17.62, P < 0.001 and F2,103 = 14.22, P < 0.001, respectively; day 6: Pearsons'r = 0.56, P = 0.003; day 10: r = 0.63, P = 0.001, and day 14: r = 0.55, P = 0.008; Supplementary file 2, a).
evidence: Statistical test results from GLM analysis

claim: On day 6, offspring solicitation and maternal behaviour are correlated with Pearson's r = 0.56, P = 0.003.
source: day 6: Pearsons'r = 0.56, P = 0.003; day 10: r = 0.63, P = 0.001, and day 14: r = 0.55, P = 0.008; Supplementary file 2, a).
evidence: Statistical correlation result

claim: On day 10, offspring solicitation and maternal behaviour are correlated with r = 0.63, P = 0.001.
source: day 6: Pearsons'r = 0.56, P = 0.003; day 10: r = 0.63, P = 0.001, and day 14: r = 0.55, P = 0.008; Supplementary file 2, a).
evidence: Statistical correlation result

claim: On day 14, offspring solicitation and maternal behaviour are correlated with r = 0.55, P = 0.008.
source: day 6: Pearsons'r = 0.56, P = 0.003; day 10: r = 0.63, P = 0.001, and day 14: r = 0.55, P = 0.008; Supplementary file 2, a).
evidence: Statistical correlation result

claim: Maternal behaviour and day have a significant positive effect on offspring solicitation behaviour in genetically uniform B6 offspring (GLM, F1,118 = 6.33, P = 0.013, and F2,118 = 6.33, P < 0.001).
source: We found that maternal behaviour and day have a significant positive effect on offspring solicitation behaviour (GLM, F1,118 = 6.33, P = 0.013, and F2,118 = 6.33, P < 0.001; Supplementary file 2, b).
evidence: Statistical test results from GLM analysis

claim: Variation in maternal behaviour influences the level of solicitation in genetically uniform offspring.
source: While one might generally assume that mothers behave in response to offspring solicitation behaviour, these results show, perhaps surprisingly, that variation in maternal behaviour influences the level of solicitation: here, we need to remember that there is no variation in offspring genotype so we assume that across families differences in offspring behaviour are due to differences in the genotype of their adoptive mothers.
evidence: Inference from experimental design where offspring genotype is constant

claim: Coadaptation models make specific predictions about how parental and offspring traits are correlated.
source: This correlation has been analysed in coadaptation models, which make specific predictions about how parental and offspring traits are correlated, and in empirical work (Kölliker et al., 2000; Agrawal et al., 2001; Curley et al., 2004; Lock et al., 2004; Kölliker et al., 2005; Hinde et al., 2010; Meunier and Kölliker, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to theoretical and empirical work

claim: Prior experimental studies have found both a positive correlation between offspring solicitation and parental traits in Parus major and Nicrophorus vespilloides.
source: Prior experimental studies have found both a positive (Parus major; Kölliker et al., 2000: Nicrophorus vespilloides; Lock et al., 2004) and negative correlation between offspring solicitation and parental traits (Sehirus cinctus; Agrawal et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kölliker et al. (2000) and Lock et al. (2004)

claim: Prior experimental studies have found a negative correlation between offspring solicitation and parental traits in Sehirus cinctus.
source: Prior experimental studies have found both a positive (Parus major; Kölliker et al., 2000: Nicrophorus vespilloides; Lock et al., 2004) and negative correlation between offspring solicitation and parental traits (Sehirus cinctus; Agrawal et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Agrawal et al. (2001)

claim: A negative correlation was found between offspring solicitation and parental traits in this study.
source: In our study, we found a negative correlation.
evidence: Summary statement of study findings

claim: A negative correlation was found between BXD offspring short-term weight gain and the corresponding provisioning of their biological (BXD) mothers on day 10 (GLM, F1,32 = 4.77, P = 0.036; r = -0.34).
source: When we measured short-term provisioning, we found a negative correlation between BXD offspring short-term weight gain and the corresponding provisioning of their biological (BXD) mothers on day 10, as well as a negative correlation between BXD offspring solicitation and the corresponding provisioning of their biological (BXD) mothers on day 14 (GLM, F1,32 = 4.77, P = 0.036; r = -0.34 and GLM, F1,28 = 8.046, P = 0.008, r = -0.48; Figure 5 and Supplementary file 2, d).
evidence: Statistical analysis result shown in Figure 5

claim: A negative correlation was found between BXD offspring solicitation and the corresponding provisioning of their biological (BXD) mothers on day 14 (GLM, F1,28 = 8.046, P = 0.008, r = -0.48).
source: When we measured short-term provisioning, we found a negative correlation between BXD offspring short-term weight gain and the corresponding provisioning of their biological (BXD) mothers on day 10, as well as a negative correlation between BXD offspring solicitation and the corresponding provisioning of their biological (BXD) mothers on day 14 (GLM, F1,32 = 4.77, P = 0.036; r = -0.34 and GLM, F1,28 = 8.046, P = 0.008, r = -0.48; Figure 5 and Supplementary file 2, d).
evidence: Statistical analysis result shown in Figure 5

claim: Mothers who are generous providers produce young that solicit less maternal resources than offspring born to less generous mothers.
source: Thus, our results suggest that mothers who are generous providers produce young that solicit less maternal resources than offspring born to less generous mothers.
evidence: Interpretation of negative correlation results

claim: A negative correlation between maternal provisioning and offspring solicitation is predicted to occur when maternal traits are predominantly under selection as long as parents respond to offspring demand.
source: Such a negative correlation is predicted to occur when maternal traits are predominantly under selection as long as parents respond to offspring demand (which we have shown above; Kölliker et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kölliker et al. (2005) and reference to study results

claim: Each BXD line is characterized by a unique combination of offspring and maternal behaviours where higher maternal provisioning is correlated with lower offspring solicitation.
source: One scenario to explain this negative correlation might be that each BXD line, i.e. genotype, is characterized by a unique (to this line, everything else being equal) combination of offspring and maternal behaviours where higher maternal provisioning is correlated with lower offspring solicitation.
evidence: Interpretation and speculation about the mechanism underlying observed correlations

claim: The negative correlation between maternal provisioning and offspring solicitation may be due to the cost of increased solicitation reflected in reduced bodyweight for the effort expended.
source: This may be due to the cost of increased solicitation (reflected in reduced bodyweight for the effort expended) for which we found evidence in our study.
evidence: Interpretation based on data showing bodyweight-solicitation correlation

claim: Bodyweight is negatively correlated with the level of offspring solicitation (GLM, F1,66 = 20.57, P < 0.001).
source: Bodyweight is indeed negatively correlated with the level of offspring solicitation (GLM, F1,66 = 20.57, P < 0.001 e.g. day 10, r = -0.39, and day 14, r = -0.44; Figure 6 and Supplementary file 2, e).
evidence: Statistical analysis result shown in Figure 6

claim: On day 10, bodyweight and offspring solicitation are negatively correlated with r = -0.39.
source: Bodyweight is indeed negatively correlated with the level of offspring solicitation (GLM, F1,66 = 20.57, P < 0.001 e.g. day 10, r = -0.39, and day 14, r = -0.44; Figure 6 and Supplementary file 2, e).
evidence: Statistical correlation result shown in Figure 6

claim: On day 14, bodyweight and offspring solicitation are negatively correlated with r = -0.44.
source: Bodyweight is indeed negatively correlated with the level of offspring solicitation (GLM, F1,66 = 20.57, P < 0.001 e.g. day 10, r = -0.39, and day 14, r = -0.44; Figure 6 and Supplementary file 2, e).
evidence: Statistical correlation result shown in Figure 6

claim: Genes expressed in offspring can indirectly influence the quality of maternal behaviour and thus offspring fitness.
source: Our study of the genetics underlying family interactions has revealed that genes expressed in offspring can indirectly influence the quality of maternal behaviour and thus offspring fitness.
evidence: Summary of main study finding

claim: Specific loci in maternal genotype indirectly modify offspring traits.
source: At the same time, we detected specific loci in maternal genotype that indirectly modify offspring traits, which shows that IGEs can be an important component of the genetic architecture of complex traits (Bijma and Wade, 2008).
evidence: Summary of genetic mapping results

claim: Indirect genetic effects (IGEs) can be an important component of the genetic architecture of complex traits.
source: At the same time, we detected specific loci in maternal genotype that indirectly modify offspring traits, which shows that IGEs can be an important component of the genetic architecture of complex traits (Bijma and Wade, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bijma and Wade (2008) and study results

claim: Postnatal cross-fostering controls for postnatal maternal effects.
source: We note that while postnatal cross-fostering controls for postnatal maternal effects, prenatal maternal effects can only be addressed (to some degree) by embryo transfer (e.g. Cowley et al., 1989), a procedure that is impractical in genetics experiments.
evidence: Discussion of methodological limitations with citation to Cowley et al. (1989)

claim: Prenatal maternal effects can only be addressed (to some degree) by embryo transfer, a procedure that is impractical in genetics experiments.
source: We note that while postnatal cross-fostering controls for postnatal maternal effects, prenatal maternal effects can only be addressed (to some degree) by embryo transfer (e.g. Cowley et al., 1989), a procedure that is impractical in genetics experiments.
evidence: Discussion of methodological limitations with citation to Cowley et al. (1989)

claim: Prenatal maternal effects may strengthen or weaken effects of BXD genotype on B6 maternal phenotype.
source: Potentially, this may strengthen or weaken, for example, effects of BXD genotype on B6 maternal phenotype.
evidence: Speculation about potential confounding effects

claim: Pre-natal maternal effects may contribute to a phenotypic correlation between parent and biological offspring traits.
source: At the same time, pre-natal maternal effects may also contribute to a phenotypic correlation between parent and biological offspring traits, as reported above on coadaptation.
evidence: Speculation about potential confounding effects

claim: In-utero effect variation due to differences in BXD genotype may contribute to differences in BXD offspring behaviour, in turn affecting the behaviour of their adoptive mothers.
source: In-utero effect variation due to differences in BXD genotype may therefore contribute to differences in BXD offspring behaviour, in turn affecting the behaviour of their adoptive mothers.
evidence: Speculation about potential mechanisms

claim: Levels of maternal provisioning and offspring solicitation are unique to specific genotypes.
source: By controlling for genetic variation in either mothers or offspring we have been able to show that levels of maternal provisioning and offspring solicitation are unique to specific genotypes (here each BXD line) and that solicitation is costly.
evidence: Summary of study findings

claim: Solicitation is costly.
source: By controlling for genetic variation in either mothers or offspring we have been able to show that levels of maternal provisioning and offspring solicitation are unique to specific genotypes (here each BXD line) and that solicitation is costly.
evidence: Based on negative correlation between solicitation and bodyweight

claim: The BXD panel incorporates ~5 million segregating SNPs, 500,000 insertions and deletions, and 55,000 copy-number variants.
source: The BXD panel incorporates ~5 million segregating SNPs, 500,000 insertions and deletions, and 55,000 copy-number variants.
evidence: Description of genetic variation in the BXD panel

claim: BXD lines are used for complex systems genetics analyses integrating massive phenotype and gene expression data sets obtained across years and studies.
source: These lines are used for complex systems genetics analyses integrating massive phenotype and gene expression data sets obtained across years and studies (e.g. Andreux et al., 2012; Ashbrook et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andreux et al. (2012) and Ashbrook et al. (2014)

claim: The BXD population consists of experimentally tractable and genetically defined mouse lines capturing a large amount of naturally occurring genetic variation.
source: We used mice of the BXD recombinant inbred population, which consists of experimentally tractable and genetically defined mouse lines capturing a large amount of naturally occurring genetic variation, which underlies variation at the phenotypic level (e.g. Chesler et al., 2005; Hayes et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chesler et al. (2005) and Hayes et al. (2014)

claim: The 42 BXD strains used in this study were obtained from Professor Robert W. Williams at the University of Tennessee Health Science Centre, Memphis, TN.
source: The 42 BXD strains used in this study (1, 11, 12, 14, 24, 32, 34, 38–40, 43–45, 48a, 49–51, 55, 56, 60–64, 66–71, 73a, 73b, 73–75, 83, 84, 87, 89, 90, 98, 102) were obtained from Professor Robert W. Williams at the University of Tennessee Health Science Centre, Memphis, TN.

claim: C57BL/6J (B6) mice were obtained from Charles River, UK.
source: C57BL/6J (B6) mice were obtained from Charles River, UK.
evidence: Description of animal source

claim: Mapping power is maximised with increasing number of lines whereas within-line repeats n increase confidence of line average phenotypes, which rapidly diminishes as n exceeds four.
source: Mapping power is maximised with increasing number of lines whereas within-line repeats n increase confidence of line average phenotypes, which, however, rapidly diminishes as n exceeds four (Belknap, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Belknap (1998)

claim: With 45 lines, power of 80%, and α of 0.05, QTL explaining ~16% of trait variance can be detected at genome-wide significance.
source: With power (1-β) of 80%, α of 0.05 we estimated that with 45 lines we can detect QTL at genome-wide significance explaining ~ 16% of trait variance, which is sufficient mapping power given effect sizes of prior work.
evidence: Power calculation based on statistical modeling

claim: Power can be optimized by maximizing the number of genotypes (i.e. lines) and reducing replicates, even with varying degrees of heritability.
source: Everything else being equal power can be optimized by maximizing the number of genotypes (i.e. lines) and reducing replicates, even with varying degrees of heritability.
evidence: Based on modeling using qtlDesign (Sen et al., 2007)

claim: Interval mapping relies on 3795 informative SNP markers across all chromosomes, except Y.
source: Interval mapping (Haley and Knott, 1992) relies on 3795 informative SNP markers across all chromosomes, except Y, as implemented in GeneNetwork (GN) (Hager et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of genetic mapping methodology with citations to Haley and Knott (1992) and Hager et al. (2012)

claim: The BXD strains were genotyped using the MUGA array in 2011, along with genotypes generated earlier using Affymetrix and Illumina platforms.

source: Humidity ranges between 50% and 65% relative humidity, temperature between 20°C and 21°C.
evidence: Description of environmental conditions

claim: Analyses used trait values per pup to adjust for differences in adoptive litter size.
source: Cross-fostering of entire litters took place within 24h of birth of corresponding B6 and BXD females and analyses used trait values per pup to adjust for differences in adoptive litter size, which is a significant covariate for provisioning and solicitation as of course a mother nursing a large litter will overall provide more than a mother nursing a small litter.

claim: Litter size is a significant covariate for provisioning and solicitation.

claim: Both mothers and litters were weighed at birth and once weekly for three weeks until weaning.

claim: Maternal and offspring behaviour were recorded on postnatal days 6, 10 and 14 when maternal departure was simulated to standardize observation conditions.

evidence: Description of behavioral observation protocol with citations to Hager and Johnstone (2003, 2005)

source: After a 4h separation, mother and litter were re-joined and maternal and offspring behaviours recorded simultaneously over 15 min, using scan sampling every 20 s (Martin and Bateson, 2007).
